notes.meaning: Rehoboam stayed faithful for his first three years while he felt weak and threatened. Once his kingdom was firmly established and secure, he abandoned God's law, and the people of Judah followed his bad example. Prosperity and ease often tempt people to forget their need for God.

In the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. The writer explains that this was not bad luck, but God's judgment because the nation had been unfaithful to Him. Shishak had his own political goals, but God used him to correct Judah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Historians identify Shishak with Pharaoh Sheshonq I, who invaded Judah around 925 BC and recorded his conquests on the walls of the Karnak temple in Egypt.

notes.meaning: Shishak brought a massive army of chariots, horsemen, and foot soldiers from north and east Africa. His invading force included Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites from south of Egypt. No human strength in Judah could stand against such an overwhelming army.

The Egyptian army quickly took the fortified cities that Rehoboam had spent years strengthening for defense. Because the Lord was no longer defending them, these strong towns fell without resistance. The enemy then marched straight to the gates of Jerusalem.

The prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the leaders while they were trapped inside Jerusalem fearing the enemy. He gave them a direct word from God: because they had abandoned the Lord, the Lord had handed them over to Shishak. Their trouble was the direct result of turning away from God.

Instead of making excuses, the king and his leaders admitted their guilt and humbled themselves. They declared that the Lord was righteous, meaning His judgment against their sin was fair and true. Real repentance begins when people stop making excuses and agree with God's justice.

When the Lord saw that the leaders truly bowed before Him, He sent Shemaiah back with a promise of mercy. God chose not to wipe out Jerusalem completely, though He allowed some suffering to remain as a lesson. God is quick to show mercy whenever people turn from their pride.

God decided that Judah would become subject to Egypt and pay tribute rather than be destroyed. This hardship was meant to teach the people the clear contrast between serving God and serving foreign kings. Serving God brings gentle freedom, while serving worldly rulers brings heavy burdens.

King Shishak entered Jerusalem and stripped away the riches from the temple and the royal palace. He took everything of value, including the splendid gold shields made during King Solomon's reign. Rehoboam learned painfully that disobeying God quickly squanders the blessings of past generations.

Rehoboam replaced the stolen gold shields with bronze ones to keep up appearances. Whenever the king went to the temple, the royal guards carried these cheaper shields and then locked them away in the guardroom. The swap from gold to bronze pictured how far the kingdom had fallen from its former glory.

Because Rehoboam humbled himself before God, the Lord's full anger was turned away and the nation was spared complete destruction. Conditions in Judah improved, and good things remained, including faithful worship and recovering stability. God remembers mercy even when He must discipline His people.

After the Egyptian invasion ended, Rehoboam regained strength and continued his rule in Jerusalem. He reigned for seventeen years in the city God had chosen as the special place for His name and worship. His mother was Naamah, a woman from the neighboring nation of Ammon.

The biblical writer sums up Rehoboam's life by stating that he did evil. Although he had humbled himself during times of crisis, he never firmly set his heart to seek and obey the Lord. Lasting faithfulness requires a steady commitment rather than just temporary sorrow under pressure.

The full history of Rehoboam's life was recorded by the prophets Shemaiah and Iddo in their official historical records. Even after the division of the kingdom, border conflicts and hostility continued between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their lives.

Rehoboam died and was buried with his royal ancestors in the City of David in Jerusalem. His son Abijah then succeeded him as the next king of Judah. God's covenant promise to keep David's family on the throne continued to stand firm despite Rehoboam's failures.
